fixes.explanation: Torn clothes and sackcloth do sound like mourning, so I see why that one caught your eye. But Moses doesn't mention either one here. What he says is don't cut yourselves or shave your foreheads on behalf of the dead. I'd have picked the familiar one too, friend. I once spent a whole afternoon sure I knew the recipe, and the dough had other plans.

The land never comes up in this reason. Moses says they are a people holy to the LORD their God, and that the LORD has chosen them. That's the reason on the table. I won't go adding reasons of my own, friend, because the text already gave us the one that matters.

Chewing the cud sounds like it should settle it, I know. But the camel, the rabbit and the rock badger pass only one of the two checks. They chew the cud, yet they don't have a divided hoof, and Moses calls them unclean for Israel (Deuteronomy 14:7). An animal needs both, friend.

Right, and here's why. The camel, the rabbit and the rock badger chew the cud, but they don't have a divided hoof. Passing one check isn't enough, so they are unclean for Israel (Deuteronomy 14:7). It's like a cookie that has the dough but never made it to the oven: it's only halfway there.

Moses gives two separate rules about the pig: "You must not eat its meat or touch its carcass." (Deuteronomy 14:8) One is about eating the meat. The other is about touching the carcass. So the rule reaches past the dinner table.
Right, False. Moses says, "All flying insects are unclean for you; they may not be eaten." (Deuteronomy 14:19) Unclean, and not on the menu. It's one short verse, and it's very clear.

A tenth is what Moses says: "You must be sure to set aside a tenth of all the produce brought forth each year from your fields." (Deuteronomy 14:22) It's a share of all of it, and it's every year. Ten cookies on the tray, one set aside. That's the picture, friend.

A third is close to a number that does show up later. In verse 28 Moses says every three years Israel brings a tithe and lays it up within their gates (Deuteronomy 14:28). But the amount he names here is a tenth of all the produce from their fields each year (Deuteronomy 14:22). Three and ten can blur together, friend.

Eat it is right. Moses says Israel is to eat that tenth in the LORD's presence, at the place He will choose as a dwelling for His Name (Deuteronomy 14:23). The grain, the new wine and oil, and the firstborn of the herds and flocks all go on that table. This tithe comes with a seat before the LORD.

Burning isn't what Moses asks for here. The instruction is to eat the tenth of their grain, new wine and oil, and the firstborn of their herds and flocks, in the presence of the LORD. The place is the one He will choose for His Name (Deuteronomy 14:23). So it's a meal, friend.

Harder fieldwork would have me worn out just thinking about it, and I'm the one standing on a gold base all day. But Moses doesn't say that. He says the eating is "…so that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always." (Deuteronomy 14:23) The lesson is about the LORD.

That's the reason Moses gives: "…since he has no portion or inheritance among you." (Deuteronomy 14:27) He tells Israel not to neglect the Levite within their gates, and this is why. As Moses lays out the feast, someone is still on his mind.

Guarding gates isn't mentioned. Moses says the Levite is within their gates, meaning in their towns, and he gives this reason not to neglect him: he has no portion or inheritance among them (Deuteronomy 14:27). Nothing there about a job at the gate, friend.

That's how Moses closes it: "And the LORD your God will bless you in all the work of your hands." (Deuteronomy 14:29) It comes right after the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow come to eat and be satisfied. A promise of blessing on all the work of their hands.
